entries.change_what: Nothing changed with this finding alone, but it explains why the Oct 1 tokenisation levers moved the median little or made it worse. The chat handler tokenised the prompt (through our cache). Because the model is registered as image-capable, it then turned the ids back into text, and the tokenizer manager tokenised the whole conversation again with no cache. The fix (pass the ids through) is in the tokenise-once entry.
entries.change_detail: In sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_chat.py (hicache tree /data01/minimax31/src/0922-sglang-hicache/python), _apply_jinja_template renders and encodes through our tok_prefix_cache (added Sep 30). Stock code then, because is_multimodal is true (model_type minimax_m3_vl), runs `prompt = tokenizer.decode(prompt_ids)`; _convert_to_internal_request sends {'text': prompt}, and tokenizer_manager re-encodes with self.tokenizer([text]). Checked with mm_ids_verify.py --trace <v3 b00> --n 300 (engine image, CPU). Fix: patch_mm_pass_ids.py, env SGLANG_MM_PASS_IDS_WITHOUT_MEDIA=1.
entries.when: Oct 1 19:20 PDT. The double tokenising first showed in a py-spy on Sep 27 13:09 PDT (row stamped 20:09 UTC)
entries.mechanism: Because model_type is minimax_m3_vl, serving_chat decodes the prompt ids back to text on every request, media or not, and the tokenizer manager encodes the whole conversation again, uncached. Our prefix cache and parallel encoding sped up only the first pass; more tokenizer processes add concurrency, not speed. The second pass was the tokenisation floor and grows with prompt length.
learnings: For any model registered as vision-language, read the chat handler's text-to-ids path before tuning tokenisation. A hidden decode-and-re-encode caps what any first-pass cache can save.
When a profile shows the same work done twice, delete the duplicate before scaling it out. We added workers on Sep 27 and the second pass survived four more days.
Check that the code you optimise is on the critical path. Our cache cut the first encode to 0.013 s (<120k) while an uncached second encode still ran.
Prove an ids shortcut identical to the old round trip on recorded prompts (300/300 here) before spending GPU time; it was then adopted after a single run.
caveats: Offline timings are single-process CPU. Online, the passthrough ran only on top of the shared cache (median 0.85 -> 0.54 s, one run each); it was never run alone.
Requests with image, video or audio still take the text path and pay both passes. Their share of v3.1 traffic is not recorded in these sources.
Production avoids the double pass: its Rust frontend (DYN_TOKENIZER=fastokens) tokenises and its workers skip tokenising (page_notes gap).
The Sep 27 TPM jump also included a Triton kernel patch, so not all of 7.02 -> 12.34 M comes from the tokenizer workers.

entries.change_what: Two changes, kept together. First, each engine's 8 tokenizer processes publish every tokenised prompt to a shared in-memory folder, so a conversation's next turn reuses the previous turn's tokens no matter which process gets it. Second, requests without images, video or audio pass those token ids on to the scheduler, instead of text that is tokenised again.

entries.when: Shared cache built Oct 1 18:55 PDT, kept with tok8sh_05x (run end 19:54); both adopted with tok8shid_05x (run end 20:41, PROGRESS row 20:45)
entries.mechanism: Connections reach the tokenizer processes at random, so a per-process cache found a session's previous turn only by chance; mostly it matched just the shared system prompt, saving 32% of what one cache would. Publishing each tokenised prompt to /dev/shm as int32 ids plus boundary index files recovers 99.5%. Passing the ids through removes the second, uncached encode.
learnings: Behind a random load balancer, a per-process cache sees a session's previous turn only by chance. Share the cache across processes or route by session before judging it.
Score a prefix cache by characters saved against one ideal cache, not by hit rate. Ours 'hit' on 98% of calls yet saved only 32%.
On every lookup, take the longest prefix found in the local or the shared store. Checking the shared store only after a total local miss gave just 2 shared hits.
Keep cross-process cache housekeeping off the hot path: atomic rename on write, time-bucketed directories, deletion by an external rm -rf, no scans of cache files inside the process.
caveats: Under the current SLA it changes no pass count at 2.23 M (15/15 before and after). At 3.34 M every miss is decode (median TTFT already 0.98 s, v3_lp_cap_lpm_075x).
Tokenise-once at 3.34 M and at 1.79 M: not measured (tok8shid_0375x was dropped at 20:55; the 3.34 M baseline is queued).
The passthrough ran only on top of the shared cache (0.85 -> 0.54 s), and the shared cache only without it; the passthrough alone was never run.

Warm 200k+ prompts still spend 3-7 s tokenising in about a quarter of cases (336 requests: p50 0.148, p75 3.27, p90 4.25 s), even though offline replays hit the cache. CPU contention is suspected, not proven.
One run per configuration, and identical runs differ by about one minute (PROGRESS 19:10). /dev/shm memory use: not measured.

entries.change_what: We tried three things: more tokenizer processes per engine (8 instead of 4), a single process with a large cache, and splitting long prompts into pieces tokenised on parallel threads. entries.when: Oct 1 15:00-19:10 PDT (earlier TOKW tests: Sep 28 and Sep 30)
entries.mechanism: The cache and parallel encode sped up only the first encode; more processes add concurrency, not speed. The uncached second encode still ran on every request, so the median barely moved. A single process also carries all HTTP and SSE streaming and became the bottleneck. Parallel threads most likely took CPU from the GPU schedulers; decode and p99 worsened.
learnings: Require a move of 2+ minutes or a repeat run. Identical TOKW=8 runs scored 10/15 and 11/15, so 9 vs 10 is noise.
A bit-exact parallel encode that cut a full encode's offline median from 0.281 to 0.073 s still regressed online. Extra CPU threads can starve the GPU schedulers; watch decode too.
Don't funnel traffic into one process just to get cache hits: the tokenizer process also serves HTTP and streaming. Share the cache instead.
Process count sets throughput, not the latency floor: 2->8 per engine lifted the static frame 5.65->7.82 M/GPU; 4->8 moved the 2.23 M median only 0.94->0.90-0.92 s.
caveats: Parallel encoding was tested while the second encode still ran on every request. It was not retested on the tokenise-once stack.
That the parallel threads starved the schedulers is inferred from p99 and decode. No CPU profile of these runs is recorded.
tok8par_05x was aborted after 8 minutes; runs_v3 keeps 9 partial-minute bins (1,461 requests), so its 0.95 M/GPU TPM is not comparable with full runs.
TOKW=8 on test v2 (Sep 30 12:26 PDT) also left the median unchanged (0.90 s) and cut p99 by 25%.
Re-scored on the current SLA, TOKW=1 and 4-chunk parallel also pass 15/15 (STANDINGS); the rejections rest on the old 1 s / 15 s rule, plus decode for 16 chunks.

entries.mechanism: With speculative decoding plus DP attention, an engine's two GPUs step together, never mix prefill with decode, and run prefill first. Any prompt chunk on either GPU pauses decode on both, and our Triton prefill kernels run at ~12-14% of tensor-core peak, so more prompt work means more paused steps. Production runs attention TP2 without DP attention, with in-house kernels.
learnings: Spec decoding plus DP attention pauses decode on both GPUs during any prefill step, so faster prefill kernels should lift decode, not only TTFT (expected, not measured).
Decode-after-prefill left 2.23 M decode unchanged (76.2 vs 77.6 tok/s): reordering keeps the same prefill work. Its 3.34 M run is queued, not measured.
Settings-only levers at 3.34 M (16k chunk, block 4, mem 0.76, cache-first) left decode at 46-57 tok/s; lockstep layout and prefill kernels are untested in the engine.
Profile between levers with the engine held (serving/HOLD): one cold 128k prefill plus a 32-stream decode trace ranks kernel targets by GPU seconds.
caveats: One engine (e3, DP0), synthetic random-token prompts; the decode trace had low draft acceptance (05:05 row).
Running requests per engine also grow with load (20-30 at 3.34 M, 37-56 at 4.42 M), which slows each step; the profile does not separate the two causes.
The 2.23 M and 4.42 M points ran test v3 (incl. production-shed giant prompts); 3.34 M ran v3.1 (v3.1 at 2.23 M: 76.5 tok/s, v3_lp_05x_v31).

Production max running: 128 per worker in serve.yaml (Sep 30); the Sep 27 argv read showed 256.
DP attention off is refused while training numerics are on (fork constraint; launch.sh refuses it unless FORCE_TOPOLOGY=1); not tested with training-compat off.
decode-after-prefill and --enable-prefill-delayer at 3.34 M are queued, not measured (node_state.txt).

entries.mechanism: Training-compatible numerics force attention TP1, so each engine runs attention data-parallel on its two GPUs with a shared MoE step. With speculative decoding the DP MLP sync forbids mixing prefill and decode across ranks, and prefill goes first, so any prefill chunk on either rank halts decode on both. Paused fraction ≈ 1−(1−p)², p = one rank's prefill share.
learnings: Coupled ranks turn prompt load into decode loss: ~50% more prompt work from 2.23 to 3.34 M cut our decode 76.5 → 53.4 while production stayed ~65.
Cheap levers only bound or pair the pauses (decode-after-prefill, --enable-prefill-delayer); the structural fix, attention TP2 like production, is blocked by training-compatible numerics.
Profile the idle rank too: with no requests of its own, DP1 was 88% busy on a padded batch and mega_moe waits; utilisation hides lockstep waste.
Smaller lockstep groups paid before: four dp2 engines decoded 71 tok/s per stream vs 25 for one dp8 engine (Sep 27 21:49 PDT, M3-era v1 trace, settings differed).
caveats: Production also runs ~18 in-house kernels, so its flat ~65 tok/s is not the layout alone.

Use the replay's low-load tail as a free control: the outside-scheduler time stayed 0.69-1.02 s at 7-67 req/min, so it was a load-independent per-request cost.

ROUTE_REPIN_SLACK=16: re-pin when slot in-flight > least-loaded + 16. entries.mechanism: Arrival pinning placed each new session by tokens arrived in the last 120 s and never moved it, ignoring work in flight: at 2.23 M one engine queued 43-66 requests while three ran 2-13. A router needs stickiness and load-awareness together: arrival pinning piled load on one engine; spreading without rank stickiness lost cache (Sep 28 hash+spill 86.6% → 81.0%; Dynamo 65-71%).
Check per-slot in-flight counters every run: twice about half the DP ranks sat idle (hash-digit bug, Sep 27 23:53; arrival pinning in v2 1.0x, Sep 30 20:25).
A TTFT-median-only SLA hides routing faults: arrival pinning kept every minute's p50 under 3 s at 2.23 M while p99 reached 87.6 s and one engine queued 43-66.

Audit every proxy limit before a load test: gateway caps already turned Sep 27 replays into 105 and 8,094 HTTP 429s (caps: in-flight 64 + TPM 10 M; in-flight 512).

entries.change_what: Cap each request's prompt chunk by its estimated cost: 16k tokens up to a 44k-token prefix, 10.9k at 88k, 5.9k at 200k, 3.2k at 400k.
entries.change_detail: patch_chunk_cost_cap.py (schedule_policy.py PrefillAdder: add_chunked_req and add_one_req), env SGLANG_CHUNK_COST_PIVOT=44000; cost model chunk × (1 + prefix/44k) fitted from the live kernel profile (indexer ~7 ms per layer per 16k chunk at a 200k prefix vs ~2.7 ms for MoE + GEMMs).
entries.mechanism: The sparse-attention indexer of a prompt chunk reads the whole prefix, so a 16k chunk over a 200k prefix costs ~4.5× one over a short prefix. The two GPUs of an engine step together (MoE every layer), so one expensive chunk stalls its partner and pauses generation on both. Bounding the cost per step evens the steps and shortens the pauses.
learnings: Profile under real traffic before choosing a lever: the synthetic profile hid that indexer cost grows with prefix length.
Balance work per step, not requests: placing sessions by in-flight context (same goal, routing side) made things worse; capping per-step cost in the scheduler worked.

entries.change_what: Replace the sparse attention of generation (verify) steps with a kernel that computes the same numbers but runs the 8 draft tokens x 16 query heads of one request and KV head as one 128-row matrix tile.
entries.change_detail: kernels/sattn/sattn_verify_v2.py via patch_sattn_verify.py; env SGLANG_SATTN_VERIFY_V2=1 SATTN_VERIFY_V2_SPLIT=4.
entries.mechanism: The old kernel ran every (token, head, block) as its own work item with a full 128-row tile for 16 valid rows, so 87.5% of the matrix work was padding, and it read each K/V block 8 times. The new kernel loads each block once per request and fills the tile with real rows. Sparse attention was about 30% of a generation step; it is now about 5%.
learnings: Re-profile after each kernel win: the next bottleneck moved from the indexer to sparse attention.
Count useful work, not just kernel time: a kernel that wastes 87.5% of its tiles is the biggest lever even when it looks 'compute-bound'.
caveats: Twin halves read a few tok/s higher than the full node; full-node runs at 1.0–1.5× follow.

entries.change_what: Turn on the bit-exact verify-path index-score kernel (SGLANG_IDX_SCORE_VERIFY_V2=1 IDX_VERIFY_V2_L2D=0) on the stack with both sparse-attention kernels.
entries.change_detail: kernels/idx/index_score_verify_v2.py; patch applied since Oct 3 05:30 with the flag off.
entries.mechanism: The kernel saves about 2–3 ms per generation step on the long-context GPU. When steps took about 90 ms, that was inside the run-to-run noise; at about 55 ms per step it is a clear share, and shorter steps also keep fewer requests running, which compounds the gain.
learnings: Keep a list of 'no clear change' levers and re-test them after a large gain elsewhere.
Judge a twin against the noise of the step it changes, not only the kernel speed-up.
caveats: The NUMA twin started before this adoption and runs without this flag on both sides.

entries.title: NUMA binding of half the engines caused OOM kills of the other half
entries.headline: Group B's automatic NUMA binding restricted its host-cache memory to nodes 0-1; the kernel OOM killer then stopped group-A engines during boot.

before_after.metric: engines healthy after 25 min boot

entries.change_what: Twin v3_ab_numa_cl_1x: group B containers with --cap-add SYS_NICE so the engine binds scheduler CPUs and memory to a NUMA node.
entries.change_detail: launch.sh NUMA_CAP=1; fork utils/numa_utils.py binding.
entries.mechanism: Node 0008 has 4 NUMA nodes of about 755 GB; GPU pair n sits on node n. One engine needs about 580 GB of host memory (2 ranks x 273 GB of cache pools). The binding gave engine 3 a policy for nodes 0-1, where engines 0-1 already hold their pools, so the bound allocation could not fit.
learnings: Pin all engines or none: a pinned engine can push an unpinned engine out of memory.
Check the bound node against the topology (nvidia-smi topo -m) before a run; use explicit per-engine CPUSET/MEMS pins.
caveats: The exact mapping fault (logical vs physical GPU index) is inferred, not traced.

entries.headline: At 1.375× a larger host cache keeps more long sessions' history: uncached prompt tokens -18%, generation +3.9 tok/s, first token ×0.82.

before_after.metric: paired generation at 1.375×
first token p50 / p99

entries.change_what: --hicache-ratio 3.0 -> 3.6 (host pool 5.56 M -> 6.67 M tokens per GPU; +55 GB pinned RAM per GPU).
entries.change_detail: config only; research wf_5eb3587c-c3d #2 predicted +3.3 tok/s at 1.375×.
entries.mechanism: At 1.375× the host cache evicts sessions idle for about 2 minutes; their next turn must re-compute the whole history. A 20% larger host pool keeps them longer, so fewer long prompts run and generation pauses less.
learnings: Eviction ORDER did not matter (LRU is near-optimal in simulation); cache SIZE did.
Check RAM: full node at ratio 3.6 uses about 2.6 TB of the 3.0 TB.
caveats: The 1.0x twin of 10-02 showed no gain from more device KV; the gain grows with load.

entries.headline: KV memory 0.76 -> 0.80 with host ratio 3.6 -> 3.13 keeps host tokens and RAM equal and still adds +4.45 tok/s and first token ×0.91.

before_after.metric: paired generation at 1.375×

entries.change_what: MEMFRAC 0.80 and --hicache-ratio 3.13 (device 1.85 -> 2.13 M tokens per GPU; host stays 6.67 M tokens).
entries.change_detail: --hicache-size was not used: it sizes each hybrid host pool (KV, index-K, draft) to the same GB, which mismatches their token counts.
entries.mechanism: More device cache means fewer host load-backs (each load-back forces an eager prompt pass and stalls generation on both GPUs of the engine).
learnings: Device and host cache are separate levers: the device part pays even when host tokens stay equal.
Keep RAM fixed by trading the host ratio when device memory grows.
caveats: GPU memory headroom falls from ~35 GB to ~24 GB per GPU; no OOM in the twin.

entries.title: MoE SM cap v2: cap only where copies overlap, +4.4 tok/s at 1.375× (bit-exact)
entries.headline: Capping the persistent MoE kernel at 144 of 148 SMs only in graph steps and copy-overlap steps removes the copy stall without the 4-5% prompt cost of v1.

before_after.metric: paired generation at 1.375×
v1 cap (always 144) clean prompt cost

entries.change_what: SGLANG_MEGA_MOE_SM_CAP_MODE=copy SGLANG_MEGA_MOE_NUM_SMS=144 (hostfix/patch_moe_smcap_v2.py).
entries.change_detail: Both DP ranks vote through the MLP-sync gather because EP2 hangs if the ranks use different SM counts; buffer layout re-checked with DeepGEMM's host query (needed an int(Array) fix found by the first smoke).
entries.mechanism: HiCache copy kernels take whole SMs; a persistent 148-CTA MoE kernel then waits for them (verify MoE p50 1000 vs 318 us when overlapped). With 4 SMs left free, copies and MoE run side by side.
learnings: A kernel gate can pass while the engine path still breaks: always run a smoke engine before a twin.
Apply a costly optimisation only where it pays (here: graph steps and copy-overlap steps).
caveats: Measured on the old base (KV 0.76, ratio 3.6); the full-node status run combines it with KV 0.80 + ratio 3.13.

entries.title: Twin side bias: engines 2-3 run ~3 tok/s slower; swap sides to cancel it
entries.headline: An A/A twin (identical configs) gave group B -3.28 tok/s; a side-swapped repeat of H2+H3 (+0.10 then +2.80) shows the same ~2.7 tok/s side difference and a true effect of ~+1.45.

before_after.metric: A/A paired decode (B - A, identical configs)
H2+H3 paired decode

entries.change_what: AB_B_SIDE=0 in the A words puts the B change on engines 0-1.
entries.change_detail: chainQ.sh and launch_tp2x4_old.sh support it; AB_B_SIDE stays exported in the chain shell, so set it on every twin line.
entries.mechanism: Some host-side asymmetry (not GPU clocks or power caps: equal SW power-cap time, no HW slowdown) makes engines 2-3 slower at high decode rates.
learnings: Run close calls twice with swapped sides and average.
Adoptions measured with B on engines 2-3 were conservative.
caveats: The bias was absent in the 10-02 A/A at 0.75x; it may depend on load or host conditions.

entries.change_what: SGLANG_HICACHE_FUSED_LOAD=1 with 4 CTAs (kernels/hcload/patch_hcload.py).
entries.change_detail: Needs the MoE SM cap: more copy CTAs than the 4 freed SMs stall the persistent MoE kernel.
entries.mechanism: A prompt pass that waits for host cache stalls both GPUs of the engine; faster, cheaper loads cut that wait and the eager-mode fallback around it.
learnings: Pair kernels with their resource budget: the copy kernel only pays once the MoE leaves SMs free.
A run-to-run spread on the baseline can sink a single-point speed gate; judge kernels by the twin.
caveats: The twin ran B on the slower side (engines 2-3) with byte checks on; the production-mode gain is likely larger.
